content:
Michael Rothgang said:

  • using an LLM when writing comments on Github or Zulip is not allowed: use your own words

Does "writing comments" include writing Git commit messages? In other words, is it allowed to submit LLM output verbatim as the message recorded in a Git commit?

For example, on GitHub in general, I see a significant increase in Git commit messages ending with "Co-Authored-By: Claude ...". The contents of the Git commit message seem to be mostly, if not entirely, verbatim copies of natural language LLM output. What is the policy on this type of LLM use for the Git commit history of Mathlib?
Fwiw, our merge bot bors only uses the contents of the PR summary, so anything in the commit messages is discarded.

Ruben Van de Velde said:

Fwiw, our merge bot bors only uses the contents of the PR summary, so anything in the commit messages is discarded.

Good point. I clarify my question to not be about the long-term Git commit history of Mathlib, but only the short-term Git commit history of a PR. For example, here is a recent Git commit message of a PR for Mathlib that is "Co-Authored-By: Claude ...":
https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/39088/changes/6f4bd5b17a6f04180b8f12769df4f5dde9b93fa8

So a restatement of my question is: is it allowed to submit LLM output verbatim as the message recorded in a Git commit (of a PR to Mathlib)?

(FWIW, I personally am not a fan of verbatim LLM output in Git commit messages, not that my Git commit message preferences are relavent here).
clarification: this is the discussion thread for #General announcements > PSA: mathlib AI policy @ 💬
Yes, LLM output in git messages are bad and shouldn’t be used.

I disagree, and don't think LLM output in git log messages is bad. :woman_shrugging:

As long as when they should be informative, they are, and they are not misleading, they really don't matter much. Certainly LLMs do a better job than my usual git commit -am "." when I'm in a hurry.
I thought we were talking about Mathlib master commit history (i.e., PR descriptions)? nevermind, apparently I can't read.
@Kim Morrison Should the human co-author read the LLM output before submitting, think about it, and make a judgement for future readers as to whether it is informative?

To be clear, the above policy does not apply to commit messages or a PR description. As mentioned above, mathlib PRs are squashed upon merge, so intermediate commits' messages are only that important.

That said, informative and succinct PR descriptions are important. Both saying too little (e.g., an empty message when something should be said) and saying too much/too verbosely (e.g., two paragraphs for a simple typo fix) are unhelpful. (I've seen this happen with LLM-generated descriptions, more than once.) It's not forbidden to use LLM help for drafting a PR description --- but treat your reviewers with respect by reviewing and tweaking its output.

A point of confusion I have as a reader with messages "co-authored" with Claude is I do not know whether to interpret the message as verbatim output of an LLM or the thoughts of the human. Perhaps human co-authors can make that more clear so readers know whether they are about to spend time reading LLM output vs human thoughts.

Firstly thank you for all the effort that went into making this policy. Secondly, I'm a bit confused that part of this appears to be a policy about the Lean Zulip and part of it is about Mathlib (it all appears in the 'contribute to mathlib' page of the website). There is lots of discussion on the Zulip not about Mathlib (e.g. about meta programming and core Lean things). Since, the comments about the Zulip I'm guessing are meant to apply broadly across all of these discussions, would it not be best to separate the two 'policies' (or combine the Zulip part more directly with the Community guidelines)?
Why not simply provide PR tags for submitters (oddly there is one: "Codex")? Propose "LLM-assisted", "LLM-committed".

Castedo Ellerman said:

A point of confusion I have as a reader with messages "co-authored" with Claude is I do not know whether to interpret the message as verbatim output of an LLM or the thoughts of the human.

I don't think Co-authored-by has anything to do with the contents of the git commit message itself. It's to indicate use of AI in some part of preparing the PR, but for example the commit message you linked to earlier doesn't seem very LLMy to me.

Ralf Stephan said:

Why not simply provide PR tags for submitters (oddly there is one: "Codex")? Propose "LLM-assisted", "LLM-committed".

We have the LLM-generated label already. (Indeed, it's odd that there is a label for codex and not other models. Though I'm not sure which way of fixing this is best.)

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Firstly thank you for all the effort that went into making this policy. Secondly, I'm a bit confused that part of this appears to be a policy about the Lean Zulip and part of it is about Mathlib (it all appears in the 'contribute to mathlib' page of the website). There is lots of discussion on the Zulip not about Mathlib (e.g. about meta programming and core Lean things). Since, the comments about the Zulip I'm guessing are meant to apply broadly across all of these discussions, would it not be best to separate the two 'policies' (or combine the Zulip part more directly with the Community guidelines)?

This policy is meant to apply to the mathlib repository, and the Leanprover zulip community. (But indeed, governance of the latter is complicated, sadly... and e.g. PhysLib is not well-represented among the maintainers or mods of zulip. I certainly don't think the current admins should unilaterally decide on a policy for the physlib stream, for example.)
This kind of governance debt is not great and should get fixed. There will be a discussion about this kind of governance debt very soon, so there should be movement on this question. Organisational work always takes time...

Vlad Tsyrklevich said:

I don't think Co-authored-by has anything to do with the contents of the git commit message itself.

I'm having trouble understanding what you mean by "has anything to do with". When you see Co-Authored-By: Claude in a commit message, you think it is written by a human and not a verbatim copy of LLM output?

Vlad Tsyrklevich said:

the commit message you linked to earlier doesn't seem very LLMy to me.

I don't understand what you mean by "very LLMy". To me the earlier example is almost certainly a verbatim copy of LLM output. I'm guessing the human author spent from zero to 1 seconds reading/thinking about the commit message. That is my guess, in general, for all git commit messages ending in Co-Authored-By: Claude. Or in other words, it is a mid-202x variation of an author running git commit -m '.' because they are in a hurry.

Perhaps the following is a wise guideline for authors that are spending many seconds thinking and crafting a commit message: change the last line to be something other than the default Co-Authored-By: Claude ... and modify that last line to be your own words to describe the commit message and source code change. Then we readers know you have spent at least a few seconds thinking about what you are trying to communicate to readers in a git commit message.

Since it's my PR I should say, it's still a draft, so currently I have spent no time on the message, but I do always check/update them before they get reviewed. Likely telling Claude what to remove/update.

Chris Birkbeck said:

I do always check/update them before they get reviewed. Likely telling Claude what to remove/update.

For disambiguation, by "check/update them" you mean the GitHub PR overall and not the Git commit message. In your usual "check/update them" workflow, you manually type input for an LLM and then the Git commit messages are still verbatim LLM output and not your words that you typed and/or directly edited in the Git commit message. This is how I understand what you are saying.

This is in contrast to what you have done for your Zulip post/message. I assume you did not give instructions to Claude to generate a Zulip post to explain to this random annoying dude Castedo :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes: what your PR process is. In otherwords, the Git commit message that you "co-author" with Claude are not like Zulip posts that you author.

I'm a bit confused with what you mean, but here is what I normally do: read the code in the PR and also the git commit message, get Claude to make any changes I think need doing. I would then submit that. So I'd likely not write the git commit message myself, but I'd made sure it's says something reasonable and I will tell Claude to change it if it's written something way too long for example.

Thank you for the clarification and details on your use of Claude to generate git commit messages. I will use this as a mental model of the typical process producing the vast majority of Git commit message ending in "Co-Authored-By: Claude ...".

Castedo Ellerman said:

When you see Co-Authored-By: Claude in a commit message, you think it is written by a human and not a verbatim copy of LLM output?

Co-authored-by: is a standard line that is a used to indicate a co-author of a git commit. It has a git-specific usage that does not specifically mean the git commit message was co-authored by an LLM. For example, Harmonic encourages you to 'cite' Aristotle by adding it as a co-author if you used it, though Aristotle as such is not really used like some other LLMs to prepare a git commit for example. I'm not saying a commit with that line will never be written by an LLM--rather I had read your earlier comment to mean that you thought the Co-authored-by line was used to specifically indicate co-authorship of the git commit message which is not its meaning.

https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/index.html
I noticed the guideline no longer explicitly ban new contributor + AI. I can see why this change was made, but I think this should be called out to keep everyone updated

Indeed, the webpage source is public, and there is no longer a hard rule against AI-generated PRs by a new mathlib contributor.

That said, I don't think this changes much in practice: a typical "slop" PR by a new contributor will still be closed, because it is low quality slop. If you're new to Lean, just using AI has exceedingly small chances of producing something good enough. There is no replacement for learning yourself.

Michael Rothgang said:

Indeed, the webpage source is public, and there is no longer a hard rule against AI-generated PRs by a new mathlib contributor.

That said, I don't think this changes much in practice: a typical "slop" PR by a new contributor will still be closed, because it is low quality slop. If you're new to Lean, just using AI has exceedingly small chances of producing something good enough. There is no replacement for learning yourself.

It is a relatively new phenomena, but I have yet to see someone actively use AI in starting Lean, and actually learn Lean better for it. There is some vague theoretical reasoning in how it COULD maybe help learning, but it seems to be exactly that -- theoretical.

I would go as far as to say that AI seems to only have a negative effect on self-learning Lean, perhaps in a structured course environment with assessments, this impact may be counterbalanced and AI can be somehow used during the students learning.

Could I ask, as an example: #38380 is a recent PR I produced which (atypically for one of my PRs, and mostly because I wanted to try out using Claude on a reasonably straightforward PR that I wanted to make anyway) I used Claude to co-author. Does this meet the criteria for an "acceptable" PR under the new rules?
I've tried to be very transparent about my use here.

The description was initially generated by the LLM (but then I lightly edited it), etc. - I essentially wanted to see if I could usefully and productively prepare a Mathlib PR I would be as happy with as a hand-authored one.

Thanks for being transparent about this. I much prefer transparency over a future where contributors lie to hide their AI usage.
If your PR is high-quality, the fact that you're using LLMs is not an obstacle. (You have been known for actually learning, and have got good PRs merged into mathlib, so most concerns above do not apply here.)

@Castedo Ellerman I can say that I am often irritating by the verbose commit messages Claude produces (and often ask it to use much shorter ones that match my normal style, which I also find easier to review) - sometimes I will just let a "Co-authored-by" one through if I'm making a small commit and I don't see any issue with what it's written.

Michael Rothgang said:

Thanks for being transparent about this. If your PR is high-quality, the fact that you're using LLMs is not an obstacle. (We have been known for actually learning, so most concerns above do not apply here.)

Certainly I think the main reason someone might object to that PR is that they don't want the new definition for some reason, and the new definition was my initiation/idea.

It just became clear that implementing all the analagous lemmas etc. would be slightly tedious. I will say that its first shot at a lot of them was still not great, it took a bit of tidying up - the proofs worked but as is common with LLM proofs that I have seen they just were not nicely compact and sensible in structure.
Still, it's a lot easier to work on proofs which have already been written along with their statements.

My hope is that a world where there is a place for AI alongside serious contribution to formalisation is possible, but I continue to be extremely sceptical of these attempts to kind of set it going as a first-order worker.

Do we want to communicate directly with AI tool producers? For example in #39192, the "Grey Haven's autocontext tool" was mentioned, and I suspect a recent batch of PR was from the same tool. Can we tell them not to use mathlib as testing ground this way?
I've personally found this Self-assessed AI Level for Contributions to be very useful in describing the amount of AI/human involvement in a reasonably precise manner.
Maybe Mathlib could consider requiring disclosure of the level of AI involvement + setting an upper level bound.
@Gavin Zhao imo, a good upper bound could be "Level 5: Bots coded, human understands completely." If you're making a PR, it should be expected that you understand every line and have reviewed it.
IMO many recent slop PRs contain "I read the code and can vouch for every line" as a copypasta, and the authors have no clue what the code does, they've just been told to say these magic words

That's fair. The "Self-assessed AI Level for Contributions" are only helpful if people are honest in their self-assessment. That excludes contributors who are engaging in bad faith and lying about their level of AI use.

Even for authors with good intentions, the phrase "human understands completely" is going to have very different meanings depending on an author's ability to judge their own understanding. Seems related to the difference between a non-native speaker thinking they understand a foreign language they read/hear vs when a non-native speaker is actually writing/speaking in a non-native language.

Plus there were complaints some time ago about the maintinence cohort repressing extensionality results for one-at-a-time replacement of structures with many dependent summands. Someone had the thread deleted and the link no longer functions.
@René Perry can you please point me to the link?

Snir Broshi said:

IMO many recent slop PRs contain "I read the code and can vouch for every line" as a copypasta, and the authors have no clue what the code does, they've just been told to say these magic words

Frankly I don't feel able to vouch for every line of a contribution I have written completely myself because I am fallible. So yeah claims like this are a red flag.

Castedo Ellerman said:

Even for authors with good intentions, the phrase "human understands completely" is going to have very different meanings depending on an author's ability to judge their own understanding. Seems related to the difference between a non-native speaker thinking they understand a foreign language they read/hear vs when a non-native speaker is actually writing/speaking in a non-native language.

To continue this analogy, even though non-native speakers may be bad at evaluating their own level of understanding, it is nonetheless possible for experts to evaluate someone else's fluency (e.g. in the Common European Framework).

Assuming good intentions from the contributor, it should in principle be possible to ask them to demonstrate understanding of the code. Perhaps, by explaining their work and design decisions on a Zulip thread without the use of AI.
